title: Wood Blankets Help Save Frozen Arctic Soil
title_zh: 木头毯子帮忙保护北极冻土

image.credit: U.S. Department of Energy · cc0 1.0 · via rawpixel

lead: A Canadian company has a new idea to protect frozen soil in the Arctic. They put blankets made of wood on the ground. This can stop the soil from melting and releasing harmful gas.
lead_zh: 一家加拿大公司有了保护北极冻土的新点子。他们在地上铺用木头做的毯子。这样可以防止土壤融化并释放有害气体。

preview_zh: 北极正在变暖。被称为永久冻土的冻结地面正在融化。融化时会释放二氧化碳和甲烷。这些气体让气候变化更严重。一家叫 PermaC 的公司想阻止这件事。他们用木头碎片、土壤和椰子纤维做成毯子。他们把毯子铺在融化地面的边缘。
paragraphs: The Arctic is getting warmer. The frozen ground, called permafrost, is melting. When it melts, it releases carbon dioxide and methane. These gases make climate change worse. A company called PermaC wants to stop this. They use blankets made of wood pieces, soil, and coconut fiber. They put these blankets on the edges of melting ground.

The company tested the blankets in Canada's Northwest Territories. The test area had very fast erosion. The edge without a blanket moved back 5 meters in one summer. The area with a blanket did not move. A scientist says this is very promising. But she says it is only one test in one summer.

The company wants to sell carbon credits. People can buy these credits to offset their own emissions. PermaC raised 1.4 million Canadian dollars from investors. They hope to give out credits next year. Their big goal is to put blankets on 20,000 melting spots in Canada and Alaska in ten years. They think this could stop 40 million tonnes of CO2 each year.

该公司想出售碳信用。人们可以购买这些信用来抵消自己的排放。PermaC 从投资者那里筹集了140万加元。他们希望明年发放信用。他们的宏大目标是在十年内在加拿大和阿拉斯加的2万个融化点铺上毯子。他们认为这每年可以阻止4000万吨二氧化碳。

The Arctic is getting warmer. The frozen ground, called permafrost, is melting. When it melts, it releases carbon dioxide and methane. These gases make climate change worse. A company called PermaC wants to stop this. They use blankets made of wood pieces, soil, and coconut fiber. They put these blankets on the edges of melting ground.

The company tested the blankets in Canada's Northwest Territories. The test area had very fast erosion. The edge without a blanket moved back 5 meters in one summer. The area with a blanket did not move. A scientist says this is very promising. But she says it is only one test in one summer.

The company wants to sell carbon credits. People can buy these credits to offset their own emissions. PermaC raised 1.4 million Canadian dollars from investors. They hope to give out credits next year. Their big goal is to put blankets on 20,000 melting spots in Canada and Alaska in ten years. They think this could stop 40 million tonnes of CO2 each year.

title_original: Woody ‘blankets’ are being deployed on Arctic permafrost to reduce carbon emissions
body_original:
NEWS
08 October 2026
Woody ‘blankets’ are being deployed on Arctic permafrost to reduce carbon emissions
A start-up company is testing whether stabilizing areas of rapidly eroding permafrost can prevent greenhouse-gas emissions.
By
James Dinneen
James Dinneen

A Canadian start-up firm is developing a way to prevent greenhouse-gas emissions from permafrost by stabilizing the soil with an insulating ‘blanket’ of woody materials. If the method works, it could be the first tool to directly forestall green-house gas emissions that are escaping from permafrost as the Arctic heats.
“Our goal is to make sure the carbon in the soil remains buried,” says Cansu Culha, co-founder of PermaC and a natural-hazards researcher at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada.
Earth’s
frozen environments are thawing
as temperatures rise in response to human emissions. The only reliable way to slow that melting on a global scale is to slash emissions from the burning of fossil fuels. But some researchers are exploring methods to prevent the thaw directly, ranging from placing reflective mats on glaciers to pumping water onto sea ice to thicken it.
Researchers say that PermaC’s approach is the first they know of to focus on preventing permafrost thaw and its
associated emissions
, which are estimated to be equivalent to those of Japan.
The company just completed the first test of its insulating blankets in Canada’s Northwest Territories at an area of rapidly eroding permafrost known as a retrogressive thaw slump. These slumps occur when a hill of permafrost thaws and collapses, enabling erosion to take big bites out of the landscape. This exposes deeper layers of soil to warming, forming hotspots of CO
2
and methane emissions. One estimate suggests that these areas of rapid erosion could amplify permafrost emissions by as much as 40% compared to models that only account for gradual thaw.
The company’s approach is to stabilize the edge of the slumps with a layer of wood shavings, soil and native seeds, and a burlap-like mat of coconut husks. Culha says she got the idea after hearing about Indigenous communities in Alaska that prevent permafrost degradation by planting trees along the edges of slumps. Similar erosion-control blankets are used in temperate areas, but they haven’t been used to insulate or stabilize permafrost until now, she says.
PermaC has yet to release results from this year'stest. But the blanket seems to have halted erosion: over the Arctic summer, the edge of the slump without the blanket retreated by 5 metres, whereas the blanketed area saw no measurable retreat, Culha says.
“That’s very promising,” says Christina Schaedel, a permafrost scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Falmouth, Massachusetts, who has been advising the company. However, the result is from only one slump over one summer, she adds.
Green blanket
One challenge is calculating how much CO
2
the blankets prevent from being emitted. Measuring the CO
2
emissions from slumps is not straightforward and remains an active research question, says Mark Lara, a biologist who studies permafrost landscapes at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. “There definitely are slumps that are spewing out carbon,” he says. But there are “lots of minutiae that could dramatically impact the results”, he adds. For instance, the emissions from any given slump depend on its geometry, the amount of carbon in the soil and how much of that carbon ends up as CO
2
or methane after erosion.
So far, Culha has only rough estimates for the emissions that the blankets might prevent. Extrapolating from research on erosion rates and soil carbon in the Arctic, she thinks that about 2,200 tonnes of CO
2
a year might be prevented from being emitted at the average carbon-rich slump. If those calculations are accurate and the blankets can be installed at 20,000 slumps across Canada and Alaska — the company’s ambitious goal over the next decade — she estimates that they might prevent about 40 million tonnes of CO
2
emissions a year, roughly equivalent to the annual emissions of Hungary.
Culha says the company is developing a detailed methodology that a third party could use to verify prevented emissions, which would be necessary for the company to sell carbon credits for emissions the blankets prevent. People could purchase those credits to offset emissions elsewhere. The firm aims to issue credits as soon as next year, and has so far raised Can$1.4 million (US$1 million) from investors, says Culha.
